title: What Trident Is
description: Start with the README. Trident is a small web page that runs only on your own computer. You ask for something once, a Lead agent writes a plan, and after you approve it, AI workers from different companies (Claude, Codex, OpenRouter models) build it and check each other's work. The README also lists the extras covered later in this tour: workplaces, the Library, Ask several, and approvals.

title: The Plan Behind It
description: The design document describes the intended flow: Lead plans, you approve, workers build, a different vendor cross-checks, and the result is merged. It also names the engine parts you will meet next and splits the work into milestones M1-M4. The teardown note compares three other agent tools (Band, Coral, PandaOS) and records which ideas Trident borrowed from each.

title: The Front Door
description: Running `npm start` (set up in package.json) or the Claude Code launch config starts one file: server.mjs. It is a local web server at 127.0.0.1:4317 that connects every other part, then sends a live stream of events to the page and accepts button clicks such as approvals, plan decisions and Library saves. Think of it as the switchboard: almost everything in the tour gets plugged in here.
languageLesson: The server pushes updates with server-sent events (SSE): the page opens one long-lived connection to /events and the server keeps writing new messages into it. Clicks go the other way as ordinary POST requests.

title: Workplaces and Settings
description: The server hands most of the work to workplaces.mjs. Each workplace is a separate studio with its own folder, board, Lead, team and Ask-several helper, saved in data/workplaces.json; removing one archives it rather than deleting its files. settings.mjs holds the few Trident-wide choices, such as the maximum number of workers per workplace.

title: The Board
description: Every workplace keeps a board: a small SQLite database holding goals, the tasks inside them, and team talk messages. It also writes a short [state] summary that is fed to the Lead so it always knows where things stand. This is the shared memory that the Lead and the workers both read and update.
languageLesson: Trident uses node:sqlite, the SQLite database built into Node.js 26, so no separate database server is needed. That is why the README asks for Node 26 or newer.

title: The Lead Plans
description: lead.mjs runs the Lead as one long conversation with Claude that stays open between your messages. The Lead never edits the board directly: it can only use the tools in board-tools.mjs, such as propose_plan, assign_task, accept_task and reject_task. Each tool checks its input first, so the board stays tidy even if the model makes a mistake.
languageLesson: These tools are an in-process MCP server. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is a standard way to describe tools a model may call; 'in-process' means the tools live inside Trident itself instead of in a separate program.

title: Approvals for Risky Commands
description: When an agent wants to do something risky, gate.mjs pauses that action until you choose: allow once, deny, always allow, or always deny. The 'always' choices are saved to a file for that exact operation, so you are not asked twice. In the page, these waiting requests appear in the Needs-you bar.

title: Workers From Different Vendors
description: These three files let Trident talk to each AI vendor in the same simple way: send a message, get a reply. claude.mjs wraps the Claude Agent SDK and uses your Claude login (it removes stray API settings so it stays on your subscription). codex.mjs keeps one Codex program running in the background, and openrouter.mjs reads your key and model and points a Claude-style worker at OpenRouter instead.
languageLesson: codex.mjs talks to the Codex app-server using JSON-RPC over stdio: each request is a small JSON message written to the other program's input, and replies come back on its output, matched by an id number.

title: The Team Builds and Cross-Checks
description: team.mjs is the heart of the work: it gives each Lead task to a worker, has a model from a different vendor review the result, and then merges or rejects it. git.mjs gives each task its own copy of the project (a git worktree on its own branch), so workers never trip over each other. talk-tools.mjs lets workers leave messages for the team that are read the next time someone looks, so nobody is interrupted.
languageLesson: A git worktree is a second working folder attached to the same repository, checked out on a different branch. Many tasks can be edited at once without touching the main folder until a merge.

title: The Library of Notes
description: The Library is a plain folder of Markdown notes sorted into sections, which every agent can read. library.mjs makes sure any change is saved as a draft first and only becomes the real note when you press Save; the replaced version is kept under .old. library-tools.mjs gives the Lead and workers the list, read and write tools for it, built the same way as the board tools in Step 6.

title: Ask Several Models
description: compare.mjs powers the Ask several feature. It sends one question to up to four models at once (Claude, Codex, or any OpenRouter model) and returns each answer with its time and cost, so you can compare them side by side. It reuses the Claude adapter from Step 8.

title: The Web Page
description: Everything you see lives in one file, index.html: the workplace sidebar, the Lead chat, the Needs-you approvals bar, the task board, team talk, the Library and Settings, and the Ask-several columns. A script inside it listens to the server's event stream from Step 3 and sends your clicks back. ember.css is the Ember design system that gives it its dark, warm look and its buttons, cards and tabs.
languageLesson: ember.css defines colours once as CSS variables (design tokens) using oklch, a colour format where equal number steps look like equal changes in brightness. Components then reuse those variables, so the look stays consistent.

title: Test Scripts and Probes
description: The spikes folder holds small standalone scripts used to try things out before building them in. e2e-team.mjs runs a full request against the live server, auto-approving everything, and logs what happens until the goal is done. The others confirm that a Claude login works and that an OpenRouter key and model are valid, without spending money.
